You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

# Continual-ARC task-1303b937 — grid-corner decoding (confirmed 2026-10-20)

## Rule
The input is an enlarged lattice: a regular set of horizontal and vertical separator lines surrounds large uniform interior areas. Identify the repeated line coordinates and the uniform interior/fill color. At every pair of adjacent horizontal lines and pair of adjacent vertical lines, form a candidate output cell from the four separator-crossing corner values. If all four corner values are the same non-fill marker color, put that color in the candidate cell; otherwise leave the candidate as the interior/fill color. Finally, trim the candidate output to the tight bounding box of cells that differ from the fill color. Preserve a 1x1 output when that is the remaining box.

In these examples the line crossings can be read where the periodic horizontal and vertical separator bands intersect. The broad regions between them are uniform fill. Do not output the input separator grid itself, and do not guess output dimensions by retaining blank candidate rows/columns: crop the all-fill margins.

## Confirmed test
Test input 17x23 has fill color 3; separators at rows 2 and 15, and columns 4, 10, 16, 22. There is one candidate output row and three candidate columns. The four corners formed by rows 2/15 and cols 4/10 are all 6, so candidate cell 0 is 6. The next candidate column (cols 10/16) has mismatched corners, hence fill 3; the last (cols 16/22) is not a non-fill marker. Cropping the fill margins leaves `[[6]]`, confirmed CORRECT.

## Demo checks
- Demo 1: fill 8. Matching 2x2 corner-marker blocks decode to 5 at output (0,0), 1 at (0,5), 1 at (2,0), 0 at (2,2), 0 at (3,3), and 9 at (3,5); all other output cells are 8. The all-fill trailing candidate column is cropped, producing 4x6.
- Demo 2: the four corners of its one candidate cell are 8, yielding `[[8]]`.
- Demo 3: fill 3. Four-corner matches yield the demonstrated 4x5 output; an all-fill leading candidate row is cropped. Output:
  `[[0,0,3,7,3],[3,3,3,3,3],[6,6,3,3,4],[6,3,3,4,3]]`.

## Pitfalls / validation
- Earlier speculative submissions were wrong largely because they guessed tiny one-row outputs without deriving the lattice or crop; test submissions `[[6,6,8]]`, `[[6,3,8]]`, and `[[6,3,3]]` all failed. Do not submit an arbitrary slice: enumerate all adjacent line-pair rectangles, decode from all four corners, use the interior fill as default, then crop the all-fill border.
- The correct test output `[[6]]` was evaluator-confirmed.

## Additional confirmed instance (22x27 test, solved 2026-10-20)
This was another instance of the same recurring task family, with a different scale and colors. The test's separator rows were `0,3,6,9,12,15,18,21`; separator columns were `2,8,14,20,26`. The broad interior cells were color 7; regular separator lines were color 4. Read the five lattice vertex values at these separator intersections for each line. For each adjacent row/column interval, write the shared color only if all four corner values match and the color is a marker rather than the ordinary separator-line color; otherwise use fill 7. The 7x4 decoded candidate was:

`[[7,7,7,7], [7,7,0,0], [5,7,7,7], [5,5,7,9], [7,5,7,9], [7,5,7,9], [7,7,7,7]]`

Trim the all-fill first and last candidate rows. Evaluator-confirmed final output:

`[[7,7,0,0], [5,7,7,7], [5,5,7,9], [7,5,7,9], [7,5,7,9]]`

The demos for this instance further confirm the same generalized operation despite varying tile scales, fill and divider colors, and output dimensions:
- Demo 1: 30x28 input, output `[[9,2,2,3],[9,2,2,2],[9,2,2,2]]`.
- Demo 2: 27x28 input, output `[[6,9,9,7],[9,6,9,9],[9,9,9,5]]`.
- Demo 3: 29x26 input, output `[[5,0,0,2,0,1],[5,5,0,0,0,1]]`.

Reusable method: first infer periodic separator coordinates and the uniform interior fill; sample the values only at separator intersections; decode every cell from its four corners; then remove all-fill outer rows and columns. Do not assume a fixed output size or keep blank margins. Equal ordinary divider-color corners are not colored markers (as shown by the all-4 top candidate row of the test).

# Continual-ARC pattern notes

## Opposite-edge bars and isolated markers make rays (task-e965a108; test unresolved)
This session reached the attempt cap with 8 incorrect submissions; no test output was confirmed. The demonstrations strongly suggest the ray mechanics below, but the test-specific combination/offset rule was not solved. Do not retain the older false claim that this test was solved.

- Grid has background, two same-color bars on opposite edges in separated bands, and isolated markers of another color. Rays paint using marker color; each marker becomes 4. Preserve bars, blank regions, and cells beyond a marker.
- In the basic demonstrated ray, paint the straight path from the marker to its nearby edge bar. E.g. demo 7 (19x10): right bar occupies rows 0–4 at c9; left bar rows 7–11 at c0. Dots in the left band paint rowwise from c0 up to the dot, changing dot 5 to 4. The right band counterpart is filled with 5 for rows corresponding to active marker lanes.
- Bars on opposite edges appear to define corresponding lanes: only lanes activated by markers on one bar side cause full-span rays from the opposite bar band; inactive corresponding lanes remain background. Demo 4 clearly shows right-side rows 0 and 2 filled (the opposite rows to markers at left-side rows 19 and 21), while rows 1 and 3 remain unchanged. Confirm coordinate mapping from each demo rather than assuming all stripes paint.
- Further observed examples: demo 5 top bar at (r0,c0-1), bottom bar at (r8,c2-3), single marker 3 at (r4,c2); output fills c0 downward in rows 1–8 with 3 and changes marker to 4, while c2 below the marker also has a 3-ray to the bottom bar. Demo 6 top bar c0-2 and bottom bar c5-7, marker 9 at (r3,c5): output paints c0 in rows 1–5 with 9, and paints c5 from marker down to bottom, marker→4. Demo 8 shows multiple markers in one band; each marker lane paints from its edge toward the marker, while the opposite band is filled across for active corresponding lanes.
- Demos vary bar orientations (horizontal or vertical in the grid), so derive each ray direction perpendicular to its edge. The edge bar itself is retained. Fill only ray lanes evidenced by markers/correspondence, not the whole grid.

Test-specific facts (unverified output): 20x19, background 5; bars color 6 at top row c9–17 and bottom row c0–8; isolated color-9 markers at (r4,c14), (r7,c17), (r9,c16), (r14,c13), (r17,c12). Every attempted test output was wrong. Failed guesses included painting nearly all cells; painting marker rays to one edge and whole opposing bands; selecting assorted offsets; and painting only c0/c9 aligned lanes. For future recurrence, reconstruct exact lane pairing from demos using indices relative to stripe starts, determine whether counterpart-band fills are on the same/reversed offset, and establish which side/band each marker ray should travel to before submitting. Keep the instance unsolved in memory rather than presenting speculation as a verified rule.

## Recolor present colors by ascending palette successor, wrapping maximum to 0
Confirmed in task-0af76fdb (one demo and one additional demo; test solved after two incorrect guesses).

For a grid containing multiple colors, list its distinct nonzero colors in ascending numeric order. Replace each color by the next larger color in that list; replace the largest color with 0. Preserve the grid dimensions and cell positions. Examples:
- Palette {5,7}: 5→7, 7→0 (demo 1).
- Palette {5,9}: 5→9, 9→0 (demo 2 and the test; test submission with this map was confirmed correct).
This is a uniform value substitution, not a frequency/background heuristic. For a one-color nonzero palette, this same successor/wrap rule would map that sole color to 0, though that edge case was not independently tested.

## Regular lattice encodes a compact grid via matching corner markers
See `task-1303b937-notes.md` for the confirmed four-corner decoding rule, demonstrated cases, crop behavior, and solved test. In brief: decode each adjacent-line rectangle only when all four crossings share a non-fill marker color; otherwise use interior fill, then trim all-fill margins.
